units.citation: Binam et al. (2015). Effects of farmer managed natural regeneration on livelihoods in semi-arid West Africa. Environmental Economics and Policy Studies.
units.quote:
The results from this study suggest that if an average low
farmer managing natural regeneration were to become a young manager of natural
regeneration, this would result in a signiﬁcant increase in the dietary diversity (as
captured through the food consumption score) by about 14 % in Burkina Faso, 13 %
in Mali, 10 % in Niger, 13 % in Senegal and 12 % in the Sahel globally.

relationship.outcome_raw: household food consumption score (FCS, the World Food Programme index of dietary diversity and food frequency over a reference week), Sahel pooled: about 12 % higher if an average low-intensity farmer managed natural regeneration (FMNR) practitioner became a new/young practitioner; pathway per the authors: fruits, leaves and other edible tree products adding micronutrients to cereal-based diets

context.practice_as_described: farmer managed natural regeneration: actively managing and protecting non-planted trees and shrubs on farmland — farmers identify and protect wildlings and stump/root sprouts, keep about five of the strongest stems and prune the rest, periodically harvesting stems for firewood and timber; households classed as low, new/young or continuous FMNR practitioners from tree density by diameter class, species diversity kept, tenure and FMNR knowledge (regeneration index); manure, compost, fertiliser trees, zai and stone bunds are used alongside on many plots
context.note: Baseline = households practising farmer managed natural regeneration (FMNR) at a LOW level (few, old trees), not households with zero trees: 'FMNR as a practice is everywhere in the Sahel and only differs by degree' (p8). Treatment = new/young FMNR practitioners. FCS = food consumption score (World Food Programme). Source of the 12 %: Table 5 (p19), caption 'Percentage changes in effects of FMNR on selected outcomes: average changes of m relative to l' (m = more intensive FMNR category, l = low): food consumption score row, low -> new/young, Burkina Faso 0.137 (SE 0.066) **, Mali 0.127 *, Niger 0.102 *, Senegal 0.129 *, Sahel 0.122 (SE 0.067) *; footnote * P < 10 %, ** P < 5 %. Under the 5 % convention (catalogue #51) the Sahel 12 % estimate is ns, although the authors call it significant; only Burkina Faso meets 5 %. The underlying treatment effect on the log score (Table 4, p18, caption 'Estimated treatment parameters on selected outcomes: average effect of m relative to l') is Sahel 0.34 (SE 0.16) ** P < 5 %, so the direction is well supported while the size of the percentage change is the weaker estimate. The paper reports no absolute FCS level for any group (only log-score differences and percentages), so no absolute amount can be given. The low -> continuous comparison is smaller and not significant (Sahel 0.088, SE 0.068). Cross-sectional survey of 1080 households (2011-2012 season), multivalued-treatment augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW, Stata teffects aipw) on observed covariates; unobserved selection not addressed. Co-practices (manure, zai pits, stone bunds) are not separated.

units.question: Your hold, answered (Table 5 (p19), 'Percentage changes in effects of FMNR on selected outcomes: average changes of m relative to l'; also Table 4 (p18), 'Estimated treatment parameters on selected outcomes: average effect of m relative to l'): FMNR = farmer managed natural regeneration (farmers protect and prune the stumps and self-sown seedlings already in their fields so they regrow as trees). The baseline is households doing FMNR at a LOW level (few, old trees), not households with no trees; the treatment is new/young FMNR practitioners. The outcome is the food consumption score (FCS), the World Food Programme index of how varied and how often a household eats over a week. You are right that the quote is about the size of the change: about 12% higher FCS for the Sahel (14% Burkina Faso, 13% Mali, 10% Niger, 13% Senegal), and the 12% is the Sahel cell of Table 5 (0.122, SE 0.067). The significance point is secondary: that 12% cell carries one star (P < 10%), so under our 5% rule it is coded ns although the authors call it significant; the underlying effect on the log score in Table 4 is significant at 5% (Sahel 0.34, SE 0.16), so the direction is solid and only the size is the weaker estimate. The paper gives no absolute FCS for any group (only log differences and percentages), so no absolute amount or baseline value can be stated. Unit corrected: Claim unchanged (positive, 12%, ns, moderate). Note rewritten per #53: Table 5 and Table 4 captions and values, baseline spelled out, FCS/FMNR/AIPW expanded, absence of an absolute FCS level stated.

relationship.outcome_raw: annual forage dry-matter production (AFP) in silvopastoral systems (SPS) vs adjacent treeless grassland or pasture, at the sites whose recorded dry year had a rainfall shortfall of at most 35% below the long-term mean: SPS produced more forage in both normal and dry years; mechanism per the authors: trees facilitate the understorey by improving its water status (hydraulic lift, lower understorey evapotranspiration) and a cooler microclimate under moderate shade

context.practice_as_described: silvopastoral systems (SPS) combining pastures, trees and livestock on the same unit of land: SPS in native forests with natural grasslands, SPS in native forests with pasture implantation, SPS with forest plantations of exotic tree species and cultivated pastures, and SPS with forest plantations in natural grasslands; compared with surrounding grasslands/pastures without trees
context.note: Acronyms: SPS = silvopastoral system (trees, pasture and livestock on the same land: native forest grazed over natural grassland, native forest with sown pasture, exotic-tree plantations with sown pasture, or plantations over natural grassland); AFP = annual forage dry-matter production (kg DM per ha per yr), cut by hand in quadrats inside grazing-exclusion cages. Baseline = adjacent treeless natural grassland or sown pasture (100% light). DROUGHT INTENSITY (p7) = how far that year's rainfall fell below the site's long-term (at least 30-year) mean annual rainfall, in percent. Table 1 (pp3-7, caption 'Characterization of silvopastoral system (SPS) sites in an environmental gradient in Argentina') gives ONE value per site, the shortfall of the dry year recorded there (21-55%; e.g. Chaco 1 27%, Santiago del Estero 37%, La Rioja 46%). Fig. 2B (p9, caption 'Mean annual forage production (kg DM ha-1 yr-1) in silvopastoral system (SPS) and treeless pastures/grasslands analysed for normal and dry years according to (A) aridity index categories, (B) drought intensity, and (C) types of forage ... Different letters indicate significant differences (p < 0.05)') splits the SITES into two groups by that value and shows normal and dry years within each. Read from Fig. 2B (approximate, bar heights): <= 35% group, SPS about 7,000 vs open about 4,000 kg DM/ha/yr in normal years and about 7,200 vs 3,700 in dry years (letters b vs a, significant); > 35% group, SPS lower than open in BOTH year types (about 3,000 vs 5,000 normal; 2,000 vs 3,500 dry). So the abstract's labels '<= 35% (normal year)' and '> 35% (dry year)' are loose: the split is between sites with moderate vs severe dry-year shortfalls, and the methods' own definition (dry year = shortfall > 35%) conflicts with Fig. 2B showing dry years in the <= 35% group. Encoded here as a drought-year claim (dry years with up to 35% rainfall shortfall, plus the normal-year reference) because the results sentence and Fig. 2B say so; severity is not characterised by the authors for this group, so unspecified. Bar values are not in the text layer, so no magnitude is encoded. Pooled across sites from semi-arid to very humid (aridity index 14-66), tree canopy cover 16.8-82.4%, so no single climate_zone. Companion unit peri24_2 carries the > 35% reversal.

units.question: Your hold, answered (Fig. 2B (p9), 'Mean annual forage production (kg DM ha-1 yr-1) in silvopastoral system (SPS) and treeless pastures/grasslands analysed for normal and dry years according to ... (B) drought intensity ... Different letters indicate significant differences (p < 0.05)'; Table 1 (pp3-7) per-site drought intensity): SPS = silvopastoral system (trees, pasture and cattle on the same land); AFP = annual forage dry-matter production; the baseline is the adjacent treeless grassland or sown pasture. 'Drought intensity' (p7) is how far a year's rainfall fell below the site's long-term (at least 30-year) average, in percent; Table 1 gives one value per site, the shortfall of the dry year recorded there (21-55%; Chaco 1 27%, Santiago del Estero 37%). Fig. 2B splits the SITES into those whose dry year was at most 35% below average and those more than 35% below, and shows normal and dry years for each. In the <=35% group SPS produced more forage than open pasture in both normal and dry years (roughly 7,000 vs 4,000 kg DM/ha/yr in normal years and 7,200 vs 3,700 in dry years, read off the bars; significant letters). In the >35% group SPS produced LESS than open pasture in both year types (roughly 3,000 vs 5,000 and 2,000 vs 3,500). So the abstract's '<=35% (normal year)' label is misleading: the evidence says trees helped forage in normal years and in dry years with up to a 35% rainfall shortfall, and hurt it at sites with more severe shortfalls. The unit was coded as a normal-year finding with no drought tag, which understated it. Unit corrected: Re-quoted from the results sentence (p10: higher 'in normal and dry years, as long as the drought intensity remained in values <= 35%'), tagged hazard_type=drought (severity unspecified, normal-year reference present), significance sig from Fig. 2B letters; note explains the definition, Table 1 values and the approximate Fig. 2B bar values. Flag: companion peri24_2 ('>35% = dry year', negative) should note that SPS was lower at those sites in normal years too.

units.citation: Peri et al. (2024). Response of forage production to drought in silvopastoral systems in Argentina. Agroforestry Systems.
units.quote:
For example, in the Santiago del Estero site (“SE”), 
the RR in SPS in native forest ranged from + 2% in 
normal years to -89% in dry years. In contrast, the 
SSP in the Chaco site (“Cha1”) showed an inverse 
response, shifting from -15% in normal years 
to + 26% in dry years.

relationship.outcome_raw: relative response (RR) of annual forage production in silvopasture in native forest (SPS) vs open grassland at the semi-arid Santiago del Estero site (SE): +2% in normal years, -89% in dry years; the Chaco 1 site (Cha1) shifted the other way, -15% to +26%; mechanism per the authors: tree-forage competition for water in severe drought

context.practice_as_described: silvopastoral systems (SPS) combining pastures, trees and livestock on the same unit of land: SPS in native forests with natural grasslands, SPS in native forests with pasture implantation, SPS with forest plantations of exotic tree species and cultivated pastures, and SPS with forest plantations in natural grasslands; compared with surrounding grasslands/pastures without trees
context.note: Acronyms: SPS = silvopastoral system (here native Chaco forest grazed over natural grassland at SE; Prosopis alba plantation over gatton panic pasture at Cha1); AFP = annual forage dry-matter production; RR = relative response of AFP under trees vs the adjacent treeless grassland/pasture (the baseline); SE = Santiago del Estero site; Cha1 = Chaco 1 site. Answer to 'is the practice worse in dry years?': at SE, yes - forage under trees went from about equal to open grassland in normal years to far below it in the dry year. SE's dry year was 37% below its long-term mean rainfall (Table 1, p5, caption 'Characterization of silvopastoral system (SPS) sites in an environmental gradient in Argentina'), i.e. in the authors' > 35% 'severe' class; Cha1's dry year was only 27% below and there trees helped. Pooled (Fig. 2B, p9): where the dry-year shortfall was <= 35% SPS out-yielded open pasture in normal and dry years; where it was > 35% SPS yielded less in both year types (see peri24_1 / peri24_2). Fig. 3 (p10) caption 'Relative response (RR) of annual forage production of SPS in relation to adjacent open areas without trees (natural grasslands or pastures) for (A) normal years and (B) dry years'. The paper's RR formula is printed as ln(RR) = ln(Xt)/ln(Xc) (p8) and values reach -225%, so the percentages are not ordinary percent changes; metric kept narrative and no strength taken. Site-level reversal kept as a separate context from the pooled units: single site, semi-arid. Absolute AFP for SE is not given in the text.

units.question: Your hold, answered (Fig. 3 (p10), 'Relative response (RR) of annual forage production of SPS in relation to adjacent open areas without trees (natural grasslands or pastures) for (A) normal years and (B) dry years'; Table 1 (p3) drought intensity per site): SPS = silvopastoral system; RR = relative response of forage production under trees vs the adjacent treeless grassland (the baseline); SE = the Santiago del Estero site (native semi-arid Chaco forest grazed over natural grassland); Cha1 = the Chaco 1 site (Prosopis alba plantation over sown gatton panic). Yes, at SE the practice did much worse in the dry year: RR went from +2% in normal years to -89% in the dry year, whose rainfall was 37% below the long-term mean (Table 1), i.e. in the authors' >35% 'severe' class. Cha1 went the other way (-15% normal, +26% dry), but its dry year was only 27% below average. Taken with the pooled result (Fig. 2B), the paper says trees help or are neutral for forage under moderate rainfall shortfalls and compete with it for water under severe drought, so silvopasture is not a drought defence for forage when the shortfall exceeds about a third of normal rain. The percentages cannot be read as ordinary percent changes (the printed RR formula is ln(RR) = ln(Xt)/ln(Xc) and values reach -225%), so no strength is taken. Unit corrected: Claim unchanged (negative, drought, narrative). Note rewritten per #53: acronyms and site codes expanded, baseline stated, SE 37% / Cha1 27% dry-year shortfalls from Table 1, Fig. 3 caption, and the answer to 'worse in dry years'.

units.citation: Blanchet et al. (2021). Interactions between drought and shade on the productivity of winter pea grown in a 25‐year‐old walnut‐based alley cropping system. Journal of Agronomy and Crop Science.
units.quote:
Under spring drought, pea 
yield was reduced in AC by −22% compared to rainfed conditions 
while it was relatively improved in AF conditions between +12% 
(when PARinc > 920 MJ/m2) and +20% (when PARinc < 920 MJ/

Tree rows 8 m apart along the slope, trees 2 m apart in the row; 1.3-m tree strips left unmanaged, peanut sown in the alleys. Plots 6 m x 20 m, 3 random replicates, 5% slope, Ultisol, Red Soil Station, Yujiang County, Jiangxi; natural rainfall 2000-2002. Table 1 (p58), caption 'Land coverage characteristics, rainfall characteristics and soil loss of 79 rainfall events for different land use treatments'. Mean runoff per event (mm): P 1.95, T1 6.37, T2 6.73, T1P 2.38, T2P 2.96; mean soil loss (kg/ha per event): P 120.1, T1 31.1, T2 31.6, T1P 89.7, T2P 81.7; canopy cover (%): P 0, T1P 58.1, T2P 67.5; tilled area (%): P 100, T1P 40, T2P 30. This unit is T1P vs P only (T2P vs P is also higher, 2.96 vs 1.95 mm, not yet a unit). So against the cropland baseline the alley systems had about 22-52% MORE runoff per event yet 25-32% LESS soil loss (wei07_1/2). Significance of these differences is not reported. The authors do not discuss this contrast; their mechanism for high runoff in tree plots (p60) is surface seals and crusts on the untilled soil under the tree rows (this Ultisol slakes), while tillage of the peanut area raises infiltration. Their headline runoff reduction (62.6% / 56.1%) is T1P vs T1 and T2P vs T2, i.e. against TREE monocultures, not the cropland counterfactual, and is not extracted as an effect.

relationship.outcome_raw: present value of incremental net returns (PVINR: the discounted extra net return per ha from switching to a system, relative to the baseline traditional bush fallow) of maize alley cropping with Leucaena hedgerows 4 m apart: N1755 per ha; the long bush fallow (25 percent farming intensity) was higher still at N2547 per ha

context.practice_as_described: continuous-cultivation maize alley cropping with Leucaena leucocephala hedgerows planted at 4 m interhedgerow spacing, hedgerows periodically pruned (about 20% of the land occupied by trees per the authors)
context.note: BASELINE (the 'control', pp359-360 and Fig. 3): traditional shifting cultivation / bush fallow with 3 years of maize cropping in a 6-year cycle (50% farming intensity: half the land cropped, half resting in bush). PVINR = present value of incremental net returns = sum over a 20-year planning horizon of (net return per ha of the new system - net return per ha of the baseline), discounted at 10% (World Bank opportunity cost of capital for Nigeria), in 1988 naira (US$1 = N5.00); scenario one = low population density, no yield penalty on fallow land; p = 0 = farmer receives none of the change in land (salvage) value. So N1755 per ha is how much MORE the 4 m alley system earns than the 6-year-cycle bush fallow over 20 years in present value; the baseline's own absolute net return is not reported. Fig. 3 (p360), caption 'Per hectare present value (discount rate = 10%) of incremental net returns of four alternative land use systems as compared to a 3-year cropping in a 6-year cycle bush fallow system in south-western Nigeria. No yield penalties are imposed, reflecting the case of low population density'. Other arms vs the same baseline: 3-year cropping in a 12-year cycle bush fallow N2547 (most profitable when land is abundant), no-till with herbicide N1712, 2 m alley cropping N1373. Labour costs would need to fall by at least 10% for the 4 m alley system to match the 12-year fallow (p360). Under high population density (Fig. 4, fallow yields penalised) the 4 m alley system ranks first (N7377, unit ehui90_9). Simulation: SCUAF (Soil Changes Under AgroForestry, a simplified USLE erosion model) for a sandy Oxic Paleustalf on a 7% slope near Ibadan, seeded with IITA plot erosion rates; maize yield from Lal (1981) yield-cumulative-soil-loss function. Ordinal use only; no currency normalisation.

No yield penalties are imposed, reflecting the case of low population density'): The baseline is traditional shifting cultivation: bush fallow with 3 years of maize then 3 years of bush regrowth (a 6-year cycle, half the land cropped at any time). PVINR = present value of incremental net returns: the extra net income per hectare from switching to a new system, relative to that baseline, summed over 20 years and discounted at 10%, in 1988 naira (US$1 = N5). Maize alley cropping with Leucaena hedgerows 4 m apart earns N1,755/ha more than the baseline in this low-population scenario; a longer bush fallow (3 years crop in a 12-year cycle) earns more still (N2,547/ha), no-till N1,712 and 2 m alley cropping N1,373. The baseline's own absolute net return is not reported. This is a simulation (SCUAF erosion model plus a yield-soil-loss function), not measured farm returns. On 'five units from one simulation': they are different arms and scenarios (4 m and 2 m alleys, low vs high population density), so keeping them separate is right, but they share one model and one source and will count as one source in synthesis. context.note: Acronyms and practices: IP = improved pasture, the BASELINE: treeless star-grass (Cynodon plectostachyus) monoculture with under 5% tree/shrub cover, fertilised with urea every 35 days, herbicides (2,4-D) for weeds, renewed about every 6 years. SPS = intensive silvopastoral system: the same pasture converted to two grasses (C. plectostachyus, Panicum maximum) with the fodder shrub/tree Leucaena leucocephala planted above 10,000 plants/ha and browsed by cattle; no synthetic N fertiliser and fewer herbicides because the leguminous Leucaena fixes N and shades out weeds (p117). Three farms (Lusitania, La Ramada, Asturias; SPS planted 2003-2004 under the GEF / World Bank Integrated Silvopastoral Approaches project), an IP and an SPS area on each, two sites per area, sampled August and October 2008; nested ANOVA (treatment within farm). Confounders the authors name (p6): pasture-management history, herbicide use in IP vs none in SPS, time since establishment, SPS area and connectivity to forest patches. The herbicide/fertiliser difference is part of how intensive SPS are managed (the Leucaena replaces those inputs), so attribution is kept isolated. Fig. 2c (p119), caption 'Comparisons between treeless improved pasture (IP) and the silvopastoral system (SPS) implemented in three cattle farms ... (c) amount of soil removed (g) ... Values of central tendency with different letters indicate statistically significant differences (P < 0.05)'. Read from the box plots (approximate medians, figure only): Lusitania IP about 1.5 g vs SPS about 8 g (letters a vs b, significant); La Ramada about 10 vs 14 g (a, a); Asturias about 12 vs 12 g (a, a). The nested treatment term is significant (F3,66 = 3.19, P < 0.05) but the pairwise difference holds on one farm only; the authors say 'tended to be greater'. Mechanism (p6): tree/shrub shade and microclimate make SPS a refuge for dung beetles; more beetles bury more dung and move more soil.

units.quote:
Cattle assigned to treatment Groups Bs and Bl fared better than those in the control Groups 
As and Al with respect to change in body weight over the course of the trial Figure 4. Over 
the course of the 107-day trial, combined mean weight gain for cattle in groups Bs and Bl

relationship.outcome_raw: cattle body-weight change over the 107-day dry-season feeding trial: combined mean gain of 4.2% for cattle fed rice straw + local grass + leucaena (Groups Bs and Bl) vs a combined mean loss of 0.7% for cattle fed rice straw + local grass only (Groups As and Al)

context.practice_as_described: living fences of tree legumes (Leucaena leucocephala, Gliricidia sepium, Moringa oleifera; Acacia pennata as thorny fence) proposed around rice paddies and homesteads to supply dry-season fodder and keep roaming livestock out; leucaena grown on-station (University of Battambang farm) and cut-and-carried as a supplement to rice straw and local grass (about 30% of the ration)
context.note: Group codes (p265): Group A = control diet, rice straw and local grass (the usual dry-season diet = the BASELINE); Group B = treatment diet, rice straw and local grass plus leucaena (Leucaena leucocephala foliage, about 30% of the daily feed, about 1 kg/day); s = the six smallest and l = the six largest cattle of each group (split by starting weight). So As = control small, Al = control large, Bs = treatment small, Bl = treatment large. Table 1 (p266), caption 'Mean weight of cattle groups (kg) at start and end of feeding trial': As 125.2 -> 127.7 kg (+2.5 kg), Al 190.6 -> 186.1 (-4.5 kg), Bs 127.3 -> 133.5 (+6.2 kg), Bl 194.4 -> 201.7 (+7.3 kg). Figure 4 (p269) caption 'Mean percentage change (with standard error bars) in body weight during Leucaena leucocephala feeding trial with cattle, Battambang, Cambodia'. Narrative kept: the effect is a difference between two percentage changes (about 4.9 percentage points), which no stated single number expresses and which a ratio would misread (the control changes sign). On-station feeding trial, January-May 2019: 24 young Gor Khmer cattle, block-randomised by starting weight to the two diets (12 per diet). No significance test reported. Leucaena crude protein 26.95% vs rice straw 5.14% (Table 2). Mechanism: tree-legume foliage stays productive in the dry season and raises the protein of a straw-based ration. PICOS caveat: the leucaena came from on-station seed/grow-out plots of living-fence species, cut and carried, not from an actual fence; the living-fence link is the paper's framing (fodder-bank effect). The authors call 2019 a particularly dry and hot year (p11) - not a named drought, so no hazard_type (#38).

units.question: Your hold, answered (Table 1 (p266), 'Mean weight of cattle groups (kg) at start and end of feeding trial'; Figure 4 (p269), 'Mean percentage change ... in body weight during Leucaena leucocephala feeding trial with cattle, Battambang, Cambodia'): Group A = the usual dry-season diet of rice straw and local grass (the baseline); Group B = the same plus leucaena foliage (about 30% of the feed, roughly 1 kg/day); s and l = the six smallest and six largest animals in each group. So As/Al are control small/large and Bs/Bl treatment small/large. Over 107 days the leucaena groups gained 4.2% on average and the control groups lost 0.7%; in kilograms Bs 127.3 -> 133.5 (+6.2), Bl 194.4 -> 201.7 (+7.3), As 125.2 -> 127.7 (+2.5), Al 190.6 -> 186.1 (-4.5). No significance test is reported. On the living-fence question: the leucaena came from on-station seed/grow-out plots of living-fence species and was cut and carried, not from an actual fence, so this is evidence that tree-legume fodder helps cattle through the dry season (the benefit a living fence would supply), not a measured fence effect. context.note: Acronyms: ET = evapotranspiration (water lost to the air by evaporation from soil and plants plus transpiration through leaves, mm); Ep = Penman potential evapotranspiration (the ET a well-watered short crop would reach under the day's weather); SMC = soil moisture content (mm of water in the soil profile); SMD = soil moisture deficit (mm below field capacity). Practice: radiata pine (Pinus radiata) planted 1990 in rows at 1,000 stems/ha, thinned to 400 stems/ha and pruned, over lucerne (alfalfa) or ryegrass/clover pasture, sheep-grazed = silvopasture. BASELINE = adjacent open (treeless) lucerne and ryegrass/clover pastures, all non-irrigated. Lincoln, Canterbury Plains, New Zealand (660 mm rain, summer drought common). Silvopasture and open pasture are two ADJACENT experiments analysed in separate ANOVAs, so silvopasture-vs-open contrasts are not formally tested. Neutron-probe soil moisture to 2 m, 1991-1996, growing seasons 2 to 6 after planting. Table 4 (p232), caption 'Soil moisture deficits to 2 m depth under silvopastures and open pasture during the third, fourth, fifth and sixth growing seasons at (a) the end of summer (mid-April) and (b) water balance and surplus moisture to recharge the soil profile over winter': winter precipitation 314 / 308 / 416 mm (before seasons 3-5) vs long-term mean 345 mm; measured winter ET silvopasture 207 / 180 / 157 vs open 172 / 149 / 122 mm; winter surplus (rain - ET) silvopasture 107 / 128 / 259 vs open 142 / 159 / 294 mm; end-of-summer SMD lucerne silvopasture 201 / 216 / 278 / 251 vs open lucerne 227 / 235 / 301 / 276 mm. This unit: fifth growing season (1994-95), lucerne pair only; the ryegrass/clover pair showed no such difference. The preceding winter had 308 mm rain vs the 345 mm long-term mean (about 11% below), which the author calls 'lower than normal rainfall', not a drought. (A presence-frame contrast was tried but the only quotable cue, 'more moisture', reads as an increase and fails the direction gate.) AWCI = available water capacity index = (soil moisture - permanent wilting point) / (field capacity - permanent wilting point): 0 = wilting point, 1 = field capacity; 0.5 is the authors' coffee water-stress reference. Table 5 (p130), caption 'Number of days with available water capacity index (AWCI) of three soil layers of soils managed under shaded and unshaded, between February 2009 until June 2010'; layers I = 0-20 cm, II = 20-40 cm, III = 40-160 cm. ALL THREE LAYERS were drier under shade: layer I mean AWCI unshaded 0.24 vs shaded 0.16 (ratio 1.55), days below wilting point 110 vs 145, days above 0.5: 110 vs 41; layer II 0.39 vs 0.19 (ratio 2.11), days below wilting point 28 vs 128, days above 0.5: 179 vs 61; layer III 0.97 vs 0.78 (ratio 1.25), days below wilting point 0 vs 0, days above 0.5: 501 vs 427, days at or above field capacity 225 vs 126. This unit encodes layer II, the layer with the largest gap and where most coffee roots sit (p13); layers I and III point the same way and are summarised by unit decarvalho21_5 ('Soil moisture of shaded area was lower than unshaded area for all depths'). Practice: Coffea arabica on one smallholder farm in Araponga, Minas Gerais, with Erythrina verna shade trees planted between the rows; baseline = the same coffee in full sun on the same slope position and management. Paired comparison on ONE farm, one shaded and one unshaded 10 x 10 m area, one sensor set per area, Aug 2009 - Jun 2010; no replication and no significance test (case study). Mechanism (p13): less rain reaches the soil under the canopy (interception) and drier surface soil pushes coffee roots deeper into layer II.
